summaryEn: At the Royal Secretariat, scribes wrote down the king's working day, every day, even the weather. Hoya learns why this giant diary is a treasure.
learningGoalsEn: Know that the 승정원 (Seungjeongwon) was the king's secretariat that passed royal orders down and officials' opinions up.
Know that scribes called 주서 (juseo) wrote the 승정원 일기 (Seungjeongwon Ilgi), which survives for 1623-1910 in 3,243 books.
Know that each day's entry noted the weather, which researchers can use today.
Know that the original is in cursive 초서 (choseo), which was later rewritten in regular script, and that fires destroyed many volumes.
Read and understand 날씨가 맑아요 (nalssiga malgayo) and 일기를 다시 써요 (ilgireul dasi sseoyo).

keywords.en: the Diaries of the Royal Secretariat

scenes.narrationEn: Let's travel back in time with Hoya to the {kw:seungjeongwon}, the Royal Secretariat. This office passed the king's orders down to officials and carried their opinions back up to the king.
scenes.artBrief: Hoya stepping through a palace gate into a courtyard where officials carry folded documents to and from a hall.

art.altEn: Hoya steps into a palace courtyard where officials of the Royal Secretariat come and go with the king's orders.

scenes.narrationEn: Six royal secretaries worked here, along with two scribes called {kw:juseo}. The scribes wrote the office diary, the {kw:seungjeongwon-ilgi}.
scenes.artBrief: A row of six senior officials and two junior officials in formal court dress and black hats; the two junior ones hold brushes and paper.

art.altEn: Royal secretaries in court robes and winged caps stand in a row while a scribe kneels in front, writing with a brush.

scenes.narrationEn: Each day, a scribe worked in front of the king together with a historian, writing quick notes of the talks. Later, a neat copy was made, and each month's diary was usually bound into one book.
scenes.captionEn: Quick notes in front of the king
scenes.artBrief: A scribe and a historian kneeling side by side, writing fast while the king talks with ministers; in the corner, a finished thread-bound book.

art.altEn: A scribe and a historian kneel side by side, writing fast while the king talks with a minister in the palace hall.

scenes.narrationEn: Every day's diary also noted the weather. Today, researchers can use these weather notes to study nature in the past.
scenes.artBrief: A diary page drawn as simple brush lines beside a small sun symbol and a rain-cloud symbol; a modern researcher with a laptop comparing notes.

art.altEn: A researcher today turns the weather notes of an old diary, sunshine and rain, into a chart on a computer.

scenes.narrationEn: The original diaries are written in a flowing cursive script called {kw:choseo}, which is hard to read. In modern times, the National Institute of Korean History rewrote them in clear, regular characters and published them.
scenes.artBrief: Two sheets side by side: one with loose, swirling brush strokes, the other with tidy, upright brush strokes (no readable characters).

art.altEn: Two sheets on a desk: one in flowing cursive brush strokes that are hard to read, one rewritten in neat upright strokes.

scenes.narrationEn: Fires at the Royal Secretariat in 1744 and 1888 destroyed many diaries. Officials worked to rebuild them, partly using other records such as the court gazette.
scenes.artBrief: Officials at desks surrounded by stacks of other records, carefully copying entries into new blank books; a calm scene with no flames.

art.altEn: Officials work calmly at low desks, copying entries from other records into new blank books to rebuild lost diaries.

scenes.narrationEn: Today, 3,243 books survive, covering 1623 to 1910. The originals are kept at Seoul National University's Gyujanggak. The diaries are a National Treasure and, since 2001, part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.
scenes.captionEn: Kept today as a National Treasure
scenes.artBrief: Long wooden shelves filled with tall old books in a quiet modern archive, soft light, Hoya gazing up in wonder.

art.altEn: Hoya gazes up in wonder at tall archive shelves where the surviving diary books are kept safe today.

facts.claimEn: Fires at the Seungjeongwon in 1744 and 1888 destroyed many diaries. After the 1744 fire a special office (Ilgicheong) rebuilt part of them (548 volumes, less than one third of those lost) using the court gazette (Jobo) and other records; the 361 volumes lost in 1888 were rebuilt by 1890.
facts.claimKo: 1744년과 1888년 승정원 화재로 많은 일기가 소실되었다. 1744년 화재 뒤에는 일기청이 조보 등 다른 기록을 이용해 일부(548책, 소실된 책수의 3분의 1에 못 미침)를 개수하였고, 1888년에 소실된 361책은 1890년에 개수하였다.

sources.quoteOrLocator: 영조 22년(1746) 일기청이 설치되어 ... 이듬해 말에 548책의 개수를 완료하였다. 이것은 본래 소실된 책수의 3분의 1에도 못 미치는 것이다. / 일기청은 개수를 위해 조보(朝報)를 비롯해 각 사(司)의 일기ㆍ등록 등 기본 사료와 관인의 일기문집 등을 널리 이용해 만전을 기하였다. / 고종 25년(1888)에도 또다시 승정원의 화재로 철종 2년(1851)에서 고종 25년(1888)까지의 일기 361책이 소실되었고, 2년 뒤인 1890년 개수하였다.

facts.claimEn: 3,243 books of the Seungjeongwon Ilgi survive, covering March 1623 to August 1910. (3,045 of them are titled Seungjeongwon Ilgi; 198 carry later office names such as Seungseonwon Ilgi, because the office was renamed after 1894.)

Every non-UNESCO URL cited was re-fetched fresh and every quote segment machine-matched, plus heritage.go.kr 국가유산 설명 text loaded from the portal's own ajax file (DATA1/heritage/hub_img/html/cul_*.html). UNESCO register pages for all four items verified via Internet Archive (registration years 1997/2001/2007/2011 with exact wording); Uigwe nomination PDF re-extracted and quotes/section numbers verified; Seungjeongwon nomination PDF could not be re-fetched (captcha) so the author's saved text was used, with other sources backing each fact. Corrections this pass: poswae schedule mistranslation (격 2년 = every third year, not every other year), 'dried herbs' removed, ep5 f4 quote exactified, 3 vocab words not appearing in scenes removed, ep5 f8 second source (정병모 판화사적 연구) and ep6 f3 festival official site added, UNESCO locators replaced by exact page wording, ep3 f7 3,045+198 clarification.

authorNotes: Character counts are omitted because sources differ (UNESCO nomination: about 242.5 million; NIKH table: 243 million). Transcription start year differs (NIKH: 1960; Encyclopedia and UNESCO nomination: 1961), so narration says 'in modern times'. Specific weather categories are not asserted; the Korean line '날씨가 맑아요' is a language example, not a quoted entry. 'Largest/greatest record in the world' claims are avoided. Revision: (1) 'one special job' removed - sources only say the juseo wrote the diary, not that it was their only duty ('junior' also dropped; juseo are 7th rank); (2) 'there is only one original set' REMOVED - it rests only on the UNESCO nomination form's rarity statement ('There is only one set of original diaries...') and no second authoritative source states it; replaced by the sourced fact that the originals are kept at Seoul National University's Gyujanggak; (3) 'rebuilt them ... and noted which sources they had used' softened to 'worked to rebuild them, partly using other records such as the court gazette' - the 1744 rebuilding restored only 548 volumes (< 1/3 of the loss) per NIKH and the Encyclopedia, and the 'sources noted' statement exists only in the UNESCO nomination form (§3.4) so it was dropped; (4) robe colours removed from the illustration brief; (5) 'scribes wrote fast' removed (not in sources); (6) goal pattern changed to 일기를 다시 써요 to match scene 6. Changes of office name after 1894 are omitted.
